# rStats.js

> R-compatible statistics for JavaScript and TypeScript: distributions, random numbers that match
> R's `set.seed()`, descriptive statistics, hypothesis tests, `lm` and `glm`, special functions,
> numerical methods and linear algebra, with R's function names, defaults and numerical results.
> Every function is tested against R 4.5.2. ESM only, no dependencies, runs in browsers, Node.js,
> Deno and Bun.

Install with `npm install @numero-uno-jpn/rstats`. All functions are named exports:
`import { pnorm, tTest } from "@numero-uno-jpn/rstats"`, or `import * as rs from
"@numero-uno-jpn/rstats"` and call `rs.tTest(x, y)`. Each area is also a subpath export
(`/distributions`, `/tests`, `/linalg`, `/descriptive`, `/numerics`, `/special`). For use from a
CDN without a bundler, see the README section "Using it in the browser".

## Translating R code

- Function names are R's names. A dot in R's name becomes camelCase: `t.test` → `tTest`,
  `chisq.test` → `chisqTest`, `p.adjust` → `pAdjust`, `set.seed` → `setSeed`,
  `sample.int` → `sampleInt`, `weighted.mean` → `weightedMean`, `pairwise.t.test` →
  `pairwiseTTest`. Methods of `glm` carry a prefix: `summary(fit)` → `glmSummary(fit)`,
  `predict` → `glmPredict`, `confint` → `glmConfint`, `anova` → `glmAnova`, `residuals` →
  `glmResiduals`. Other renamed functions: `var` → `variance`, `%*%` → `matMul`,
  `.Random.seed` → `getRandomSeed()` / `setRandomSeed(seed)`, `qr.Q` → `qrQ` (likewise `qrR`,
  `qrCoef`, `qrResid`, ...). Functions from other packages keep their own names (`zTest` from
  BSDA, `brunnerMunzelTest` from lawstat, `ginv` from MASS, `grad` and `hessian` from numDeriv).
- Required arguments are positional; optional ones go in one options object with camelCase keys:
  `pt(q, df, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)` → `pt(q, df, { lowerTail: false, logP: true })`,
  `t.test(x, y, var.equal = TRUE, conf.level = 0.99)` →
  `tTest(x, y, { varEqual: true, confLevel: 0.99 })`. When an optional second sample is
  omitted, the options take its place: `tTest(x, { mu: 1 })`.
- Option values are R's strings: `alternative: "less"` (unambiguous abbreviations such as `"l"`
  are accepted, as with R's `match.arg`), `method: "kendall"`, `family: "binomial"`.
- Results are plain objects with camelCase fields. Hypothesis tests return R's `htest` fields:
  `statistic`, `parameter`, `pValue` (R's `p.value`), `confInt` (`conf.int`) with `confLevel`,
  `estimate`, `nullValue`, `method`, `alternative`. R's names of these values are separate
  fields: `statisticName`, `parameterName`, `estimateNames`, `nullValueName`.
- Data shapes: a sample is an array of numbers or a `Float64Array`. A matrix or contingency table
  is an array of rows. Grouped data is either an array of samples (`kruskalTest([a, b, c])`) or
  values with a parallel array of group labels (`kruskalTest(x, g)`). The first argument of the
  d/p/q functions may be a number or an array (the result has the same shape); distribution
  parameters are scalars and are not recycled as vectors.
- Models: `lm` and `aov` take an R formula string and a data frame given as an object of columns:
  `lm("y ~ A * B + x", { y, A, B, x })`, `aov("y ~ W + Error(id/W)", data)`; string columns are
  factors (levels sorted by code point unless `levels: { A: [...] }`), `contrasts: { A: "contr.sum" }`
  sets the coding. Formula functions such as `log(x)` or `I(x^2)` are not supported: compute the
  column first. Tables (`anova(fit)`, `Anova(fit, { type: 3 })` for car's `Anova`, `aovSummary(fit)`)
  are `{ colNames, rowNames, table }` with R's names. afex's `aov_ez(id, dv, data, between, within)`
  is `aovEz(data, { id, dv, between, within })`. `lm(x, y)` also takes a matrix, and `glm(x, y, {
  family })` takes a matrix (array of rows) or a vector of predictors (no formula); the intercept
  is added unless `intercept: false`. A binomial response can be rows of `[successes, failures]`,
  like `cbind(s, f)` in R.
- Indices are 0-based where R returns indices: `sampleInt(n)` returns `0..n-1` (R's
  `sample.int(n) - 1` from the same random stream), and the pivots of `qr` and `chol`.
- Hypothesis tests do not emit R's warnings. `glm` returns R's warnings in its result
  (`warnings`).
- Power calculations take one options object and solve for the quantity given as `null`:
  `power.t.test(delta = 0.5, power = 0.8)` → `powerTTest({ delta: 0.5, power: 0.8 })`, pwr's
  `pwr.anova.test(k = 3, f = 0.25, power = 0.8)` → `pwrAnovaTest({ k: 3, f: 0.25, power: 0.8 })`
  (`sig.level` → `sigLevel`). effectsize's `cohens_d(x, y)` → `cohensD(x, y)` (`{ name, value, ciLow, ciHigh }`),
  `eta_squared(model)` → `etaSquared(anova(fit))` or `etaSquared(Anova(fit, { type: 3 }))`.
- Cox regression takes the covariates as a matrix (array of rows): `coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ x1 + x2, ties =
  "breslow", weights = w)` → `coxph(time, status, x, { ties: "breslow", weights: w })`, with `strata` as labels.
  psych's `omega(m, nfactors = 3)` → `omega(x, { nfactors: 3 })` (`omega(null, { covmat: R })` for a correlation
  matrix).
- Data frames are objects of columns (`null` or `NaN` for NA). Tests take formulas like R's:
  `t.test(y ~ g, data = d)` → `tTest("y ~ g", d)`, `friedman.test(y ~ w | b, d)` → `friedmanTest("y ~ w | b", d)`,
  `cor.test(~ x + y, d)` → `corTest("~ x + y", d)`. `na.omit(d)` → `naOmit(d)`, `complete.cases(d)` →
  `completeCases(d)`, `subset(d, age >= 20, select = c(y, g))` → `subset(d, (r) => r.age >= 20, { select: ["y",
  "g"] })`, `tapply(x, g, mean)` → `tapply(x, g, mean)` (`{ dim, dimnames, values }`), `split(x, g)` → a `Map`,
  `aggregate(y ~ g + sex, d, mean)` → `aggregate("y ~ g + sex", d, mean)`, `merge(a, b, by = "id", all.x = TRUE)`
  → `merge(a, b, { by: "id", allX: true })`, `rbind(d1, d2)` → `rbind(d1, d2)`.
- Random numbers: after `setSeed(42)`, `rnorm`, `runif`, `sample` and the other `r*` functions
  give the same numbers as R after `set.seed(42)`. `RNGkind` supports Mersenne-Twister (R's
  default) and L'Ecuyer-CMRG.

## Examples

```ts
import { pnorm, pt, setSeed, rnorm, tTest, glm, glmSummary } from "@numero-uno-jpn/rstats";

pnorm(1.96);                                  // 0.9750021048517795
pt(2, 10, { lowerTail: false, logP: true });  // -3.3051415512324533

setSeed(42);
rnorm(3);  // [1.3709584471466685, -0.5646981713960887, 0.3631284113373392], as in R

const r = tTest([5.1, 4.9, 6.2, 5.8, 6.0, 5.5], [4.1, 4.5, 5.0, 4.8, 4.3]);
r.pValue;  // 0.0035365308877675647 (Welch, R's default)
r.confInt; // [0.4423253334608047, 1.6443413332058612]

// R: glm(cbind(s, f) ~ dose, family = binomial)
const fit = glm([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], [[1, 19], [4, 16], [9, 11], [13, 7], [18, 2], [19, 1]], { family: "binomial" });
fit.coefficients;        // ≈ [-3.77413, 1.14807]
glmSummary(fit).pValue;  // ≈ [5.357e-8, 3.579e-9]
```
